newsitem.title: USA: USAA revives attempt to sell catastrophe bonds.
newsitem.headline: USAA revives attempt to sell catastrophe bonds.

text.p: USAA Group is back again this summer with a revised version of a bond offering it attempted last year that would link an investor's returns to the company's windstorm losses.

San Antonio, Texas-based USAA, one of the country's largest property-casualty insurers, hopes to complete the offering of so-called catastrophe bonds this month, in time for the summer hurricane season, sources familiar with the transaction said.
USAA declined comment.
In its proposed offering, USAA hopes to sell at least $150 million of the catastrophe bonds, and possibly as much as $400 million, in two separate tranches, sources said.
USAA last year attempted to sell $500 million in bonds, but in a public, rather than a private, offering.

Investors who buy the bonds could lose some or all of their money, depending on which tranche they bought, if the company's losses from an East Coast hurricane topped $1 billion this year, the sources said.
The cover would begin as of July 1, sources said.

In addition to the USAA deal, Swiss Reinsurance Co hopes to complete this month a $100 million offering of bonds tied to the industry's losses from a California earthquake over a two-year period, the sources said.
Sources said the deal represents the securitization of Swiss Re's exposure to the California Earthquake Authority.
That deal also is being sold in separate tranches; one with everything at risk and another that is partially protected.
Swiss Re was not immediately available for comment.
Both deals, which are private placement offerings with institutional investors, appear to be attracting substantial interest, sources said.
In another development, reinsurance intermediary Guy Carpenter said it plans to publish by the end of July a catastrophe index that would create a standardized benchmark for insurance risks.
The index would help both investors and insurers better gauge the potential risks and rewards associated with the catastrophe bonds.

"We think this will really help in the furtherance of the securitization of insurance risk," said Christopher McGhee, managing director of Guy Carpenter Risk Products. Guy Carpenter is a subsidiary of Marsh & McLennan Cos Inc.
The two deals and the new index represent the latest efforts underway to further develop the fledgling risk securitization market.

St. Paul Re, the reinsurance arm of St. Paul Cos Inc, late last year completed one of the industry's first securitized risk transactions, a $68.5 million deal linking investor's returns to the company's underwriting performance.
"Other things are clearly in the pipeline," one of the sources said.
In the past, insurers have traditionally attempted to reduce their risk from large catastrophes by buying reinsurance, or insurance for insurance companies.

But a sharp spike in reinsurance rates, combined with a serious lack of supply following Hurricane Andrew in 1992, prompted insurers to begin to seek ways of tapping the capital markets for protection.

Although reinsurance rates have dropped sharply in the last year or so, some insurers are still interested in developing capital market alternatives to reinsurance, concerned that the next big catastrophe may send rates spiralling upward once again, sources said.
"The reinsurance marketplace is very soft right now," Guy Carpenter's McGhee said.
"There's lots of capacity and the prices are much lower than in the early '90's, and that has actually slowed the issuance or success of insurance securitization," he said.

But, he said, "Insurance companies feel that they have a vested interest in increasing the overall supply of catastrophe risk transfer available to them and if they have to invest in R&D to help make this market go, some of them are willing to do that."
For investors, the bonds are expected to offer attractive yields with a risk that is uncorrelated with the risks associated with other securities.
